abstract: A synthetic approach to CHF 2 -substituted aromatic, heteroaromatic, alkenyl, and cyclopropyl boronates was described, based on deoxofluorination of the corresponding aldehydes with the boron atom temporarily masked as a trifluoroborate. In a telescoped sequence, formylsubstituted pinacol boronates were converted into triethylammonium trifluoroborates with Et 3 N·3HF, deoxofluorinated with Deoxo-Fluor and Et 3 N·3HF in CH 2 Cl 2 or CH 2 Cl 2 – THF, and re-esterified with pinacol in the presence of TMSCl; isolated potassium trifluoroborates could be used as well.

title: Operando conductivity tracking reveals irreversible conductivity loss in IrOx during PEM electrolysis
abstract: The conductivity of each component in a proton exchange membrane (PEM) water electrolysis is critical to device performance, particularly at high current densities where ohmic losses dominate. However, in situ conductivity changes within the iridium oxide (IrOx) electrocatalyst applied for the oxygen evolution reaction (OER), and their impact on device performance, remain unexplored, largely because IrOx is assumed to retain metallic conductivity under OER relevant conditions.

title: Collective Stereodivergent Synthesis of the [13]Graphanyl Isomers: Applications as Drug Analogues
abstract: Conformationally locked polycycles represent an attractive class of compounds in drug discovery campaigns for medicinal chemists. The three-dimensionality of these scaffolds can result in unique topologies and well-defined exit vectors, enhancing pharmacokinetic profiles and protein interactions that lead to the development of clinically approved therapeutics. One such scaffold that has remained largely underexplored is [13]Graphane, as the synthesis of its four stereoisomers is nontrivial.

title: Predicting the Host-guest Binding Gibbs Free Energy for Guests
abstract: Host-guest chemistry involves noncovalent interactions between host and guest molecules and has been applied in areas such as adaptive materials, sensing, and drug delivery. However, the discovery of new hosts and the identification of suitable guests remain challenging because selective binding is governed by subtle and often competing noncovalent interactions that are difficult to predict. To overcome this predictive limitation, computational framework was developed to predict Gibbs free energies of host-guest binding using a hybrid machine-learning model.

title: ABC-flash: Fast and Scalable D3 Three-Body Dispersion for Large Molecular and Periodic Systems
abstract: Three-body dispersion influences molecular binding and structural stability, yet its computational and memory demands can hinder routine inclusion in large systems. Here, we introduce ABC-flash, a GPU-accelerated implementation of the D3 Axilrod–Teller–Muto (ATM) correction for molecular and periodic systems. Sparse pair tiles enable reuse of shared factors and on-the-fly accumulation of triplet energies and derivatives, retaining the established D3-ATM formulation and its coordination-number dependence without storing global triplet intermediates.

title: Escaping Amnesia: A Kinetic Ratchet Records System History
abstract: The transition from abiotic chemistry to biological systems required escaping thermodynamic equilibrium and establishing early forms of chemical memory and heritable information. Darwinian evolution relies on template-directed replication, which presupposes a sophisticated molecular recognition apparatus that could not have existed prior to the emergence of biopolymers. Here, we demonstrate that pre-genetic molecular memory can arise as a collective dynamical property of chemical ratchets driven by environmental oscillations.

title: Best Practices for Unsupervised Learning in Molecular Systems
abstract: Unsupervised learning is used throughout computational molecular science on unlabeled data such as molecular dynamics trajectories and conformer ensembles. Some questions admit no predefined labels at all: how many conformational states a molecule visits, whether a virtual library covers chemical space, or which structures are unlike anything else in the set. Clustering, dimensionality reduction, and density estimation serve both cases. They are easy to apply, and their output generally appears like a discovery, whether or not it is one.

title: Hydrophobic Ligands Promote CO 2 Electroreduction on Gold Nanorod Catalysts
abstract: Enhancing the activity and selectivity of CO 2 reduction reaction (CO 2 RR) would help close the carbon cycle by converting CO 2 into a value-added chemical reagent using renewable electricity. Tuning reaction kinetics requires careful control of catalyst size, shape, composition, and surface structure. Colloidal synthesis offers a promising route to nanocatalyst design; however, colloidally synthesized nanoparticles are passivated by surface ligands that mediate access of reagents to the catalyst, block certain surface sites, and determine the local reaction environment.

title: Catalytic upcycling of aliphatic polyethers and polyurethanes into α,ω-dichloroalkanes
abstract: Aliphatic polyethers are ubiquitous polymers in pharmaceutics and essential building blocks for polyurethanes production. Yet their recycling is underexploited, owing to their strong C-O bond (BDE of ~85 kcal mol-1) as challenging reactive handle. Herein, we highlight the exceptional reactivity of gallium or iron catalysis to upcycle these aliphatic polyethers using boron trichloride as a chlorinating reagent, to offset the thermodynamic cost of creating a C-Cl bond from a C-O bond.

title: Electrochemically Directed Orientation in Two-Dimensional Conductive Metal-Organic Framework Thin Films
abstract: Controlling the preferred crystallographic orientation of two-dimensional (2D) conductive metal-organic framework (c-MOF) films is essential for maximizing anisotropic charge transport and unlocking their full potential in advanced applications. However, the factors governing film orientation during electrochemical growth on a substrate remain poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that the preferred orientation of amine-derived Ni3(HITP)2 films can be modulated by small changes in applied potential during anodic electrodeposition.

title: Cyclodextrin-Confined Boranylium Cations
abstract: Discrete molecular cavities offer powerful platforms to stabilise reactive species and modulate their reactivity through confinement. Here, we report the synthesis of cyclodextrin-confined NHC-boranes and their conversion into Lewis acidic boranylium cations. Confinement within α- and β-cyclodextrin cavities strongly affects the 11 B NMR properties of the NHC–BH 3 precursors, leading to unusually short relaxation and broad, unresolved, signals. Upon hydride abstraction, the corresponding boranylium cations remained undetectable by 11 B NMR spectroscopy on spectrometers up to 600 MHz.

title: Tissue-specific biotransformation shapes the toxicity of 6PPD-quinone in fish cell models
abstract: Acute mortality of salmonids exposed to urban runoff has been linked to 6PPD-quinone (6PPD-Q), a transformation product of the widely used tire antiozonant 6PPD. However, the cellular processes underlying 6PPD-Q toxicity remain poorly understood. Beyond the well-documented differences in species sensitivity, here we determined tissue-specific responses in rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) cell lines exposed to 6PPD-Q: brain-derived cells (RTBrain) were more sensitive than gill-derived cells (RTgill-W1). To unravel the cellular mechanisms underlying such differential responses, we combined time-resolved 6PPD-Q cellular depletion kinetics, targeted biotransformation product (BTP) profiling, transporter inhibition experiments, and cytotoxicity assessments. Both cell models biotransformed 6PPD-Q, but RTBrain displayed a 6.6-fold higher cellular clearance rate than RTgill-W1. Chemical profiling identified four BTPs, including para-aryl-OH-6PPD-Q, which was selectively toxic to RTBrain but not RTgill-W1 cells. These findings reveal tissue-specific toxicokinetics as potential determinants of differential 6PPD-Q toxicity even within the same species. More broadly, this integrated approach highlights the importance of considering biotransformation and the production of biologically active transformation products when assessing susceptibility to emerging contaminants.

title: Gene-scale DNA and chromatin ensembles with atomic resolution
abstract: The spatial organization of cellular DNA extends across a wide range of scales, from sequence-dependent base pairing to the packaging of meter-long cellular DNA into micron-size nuclei. Integrating the information from disparate experiments, molecular simulations, and theoretical models into a coherent picture of DNA and chromatin organization across scales remains challenging. Here, we introduce hierarchical chain growth for DNA (HCG-DNA) to build atomically detailed ensembles of double-stranded DNA and chromatin. Starting from complete tetranucleotide fragment libraries encoding local sequence-dependent conformations, we assemble structures of DNA up to the megabase scale at quasilinear computational cost. From HCG-DNA, the large-scale polymer elastic properties emerge, in particular the persistence length. HCG-DNA recovers electron spin resonance, atomic force microscopy, and single-molecule force spectroscopy measurements of DNA structure across scales. HCG-DNA includes nucleosomes to generate 3D atomistic chromatin ensembles constrained by cryo-electron tomography or genomic nucleosome maps. With HCG-DNA, we show how small changes in nucleosome linker length alter nucleosome packing and chromatin compaction. HCG-DNA connects atomic-level DNA and nucleosome structure to chromosome-scale spatial organization, while providing scalable ensembles for coarse-grained model development and AI training.

title: The crystal structure of the human SIPA1L2 PDZ domain reveals an atypically short, metazoan-conserved β2 β3 loop
abstract: Signal - induced proliferation-associated 1-like protein 2 (SIPA1L2) is a large neuronal Rap GTPase-activating protein implicated in dynein-dependent retrograde transport of BDNF-TrkB signaling endosomes and genetically linked to Parkinson's disease. It consists of a RapGAP domain, a PDZ domain, and a coiled-coil domain separated by intrinsically disordered regions. Its compact PDZ domain mediates protein-protein interaction by binding short PDZ-binding motifs (PBM) in target proteins. Here, the human SIPA1L2 PDZ domain (residues 943-1027) was crystallized and its structure determined by molecular replacement. The domain adopts the canonical PDZ fold of six beta-strands forming two antiparallel beta-sheets flanked by two alpha-helices. The beta 2 - beta 3 loop, located next to the PBM binding groove, is unusually short - eight residues, against a 14-residue human-PDZome consensus. A BLASTP- and AlphaFold3-based survey across Metazoa shows that, despite PDZ sequence identities falling to ~25 %, the fold and the short loop are structurally conserved (Calpha; RMSD 0.5 - 0.8 Angstrom), indicating that this is a genuine, evolutionarily constrained architectural feature of SIPA1L2-type PDZ domains. PBM binding was not observed in co-crystallization trials. Native holdup assays against a neuronal proteome identified no specific partners for the SIPA1L2 PDZ domain. The structure retains the canonical carboxylate-binding loop and a class-I-type histidine, so partner scarcity is not due to loss of the PBM binding apparatus. Impaired PBM binding seems to result from the combination of the unusually short beta 2 - beta 3 loop and an evolutionarily invariant His964 located at the beta 2 strand. The short loop might restrict the conformational dynamics of the beta 2 strand, thereby stabilizing His964 side-chain conformations that encroach on the PBM binding groove. The structure thus defines SIPA1L2 as a structurally canonical yet apparently orphan PDZ domain.

title: Pharmacolibrary: Interoperable executable models for PK, PD and PGx derived from published evidence
abstract: Published pharmacological knowledge is distributed across heterogeneous scientific literature, databases, and computational models, making systematic reuse, comparison, and reproducibility difficult. We present Pharmacolibrary v26.11, a source-traceable resource that connects pharmacokinetic (PK), pharmacodynamic (PD), and pharmacogenomic (PGx) knowledge with executable models, simulations, and interactive visualizations. A multi-agent workflow combines LLM-assisted literature retrieval and extraction with deterministic validation, ontology mapping, provenance tracking, automated model generation, and rule-based review. The system transforms published evidence and extracted parameters into executable models across Modelica, FMI, SBML, MATLAB, and CellML and provides browser-based simulations for research and education. Preliminary evaluation indicates that decomposing literature extraction into multiple stages improves parameter recovery compared with single-pass extraction and that locally deployed open-weight models can provide performance that is at least comparable with frontier commercial LLMs. Pharmacolibrary provides a foundation for scalable, auditable curation of pharmacological knowledge and for connecting published evidence to reusable computational models across research, simulation, and education.

title: Automated segmentation of renal structures using brightfield images of unstained kidney biopsies
abstract: The automated segmentation of unstained kidney brightfield microscopy images remains a significant challenge in medical imaging. In conventional histopathology, staining provides crucial structural and molecular contrast, allowing renal compartments and structures to be readily distinguished. The absence of staining markedly reduces this contrast, obscuring the fine architectural details that are essential for diagnosis.

title: Native-like 3D colonoids reveal mechanisms of colonic drug disposition
abstract: Intestinal organoid research in drug absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity (ADME-T) has focused predominantly on small intestinal enteroids, leaving colonic drug handling comparatively unexplored. Here, we established and characterized adult colonic stem cell-based three-dimensional (3D) organoid (colonoid) models as physiologically relevant New Approach Methodologies (NAMs). Donor-matched mucosal tissue, isolated primary epithelial cells, and 3D colonoids were characterized using global and targeted proteomics, fixed and live-cell microscopy, functional ADME-T assays and targeted lipidomics. This complementary analysis identified isolated primary epithelial cells as a more representative native epithelial reference than excised mucosal tissue. Suspended differentiated apical- and basal-out colonoid configurations more closely matched this reference across the assessed characteristics. Together, these two configurations provided access to both apical and basolateral epithelial surfaces, enabling functional studies of key drug transporters (P-gp, BCRP) and metabolizing enzymes (CYP3A4, UGT1A, SULT1A) in a native-like setting. Measurement of intracellular bioavailability (Fic), reflecting drug availability to intracellular targets, revealed lipophilicity-dependent microvillar absorption mechanisms. Hydrophilic compounds exploited the enlarged membrane surface provided by microvilli, whereas highly permeable lipophilic compounds seemingly entered only at the microvillus tips. Compared with HEK293 cells, an established reference model for Fic measurements, colonoids combined native-like epithelial geometry with higher phospholipid content and generally stronger intracellular drug binding, highlighting the importance of both architecture and cellular composition for studying colonic drug disposition. These colonoid models provide a physiologically relevant platform for investigating colonic ADME-T and reveal how microvillar architecture shapes intracellular drug bioavailability.

title: Gut Microbial Butyrate Metabolism Generates an N-Acyl Amide that Regulates Host Transcriptional Programs
abstract: Faecalibacterium prausnitzii is a prominent member of the human gut microbiota whose depletion is associated with various intestinal and metabolic disorders. While multiple mechanisms have been proposed to explain how F. prausnitzii promotes host health, the molecular determinants underlying these activities remain elusive. Here, we show that F. prausnitzii is a prolific producer of the human metabolite N-butyrylglycine, which we find accumulates to millimolar concentrations in bacterial culture and is readily detectable in the feces of conventional wildtype mice. We establish an enzymatic basis of N-butyrylglycine production by identifying and biochemically validating an F. prausnitzii N-acyltransferase that catalyzes the conjugation of butyryl-CoA and glycine. Despite being derived from butyrate, N-butyrylglycine exhibits distinct bioactivity from its precursor, including reduced histone deacetylase inhibitory activity, an altered inflammatory profile, and enhanced suppression of cellular proliferation across multiple cancer cell lines. Furthermore, transcriptomic profiling revealed N butyrylglycine coordinates repression of G2/M checkpoint-associated programs and downregulation of the colorectal cancer associated gene AOC1. Together, these findings suggest that specialized metabolites produced by F. prausnitzii contribute to its beneficial effects and may underlie its protective role in colorectal cancer.

title: Coming US biosecurity screening for DNA purchases spurs concerns
abstract: Scientists worry the policy will do more to slow valuable research than to address bioweapon issues

title: Phosphorylation elicits bifurcated regulation of NaV1.5 by intracellular auxiliary proteins
abstract: The cardiac sodium channel Nav1.5 carries the upstroke of the cardiac action potential, and its inactivation needs to be precisely controlled: shifts of only a few millivolts in steady-state inactivation (SSI), or incomplete pore closure generating a late current, are arrhythmogenic. Inactivation is modulated by both tyrosine phosphorylation and protein-protein interactions, but whether or how the two intersect is unclear. Combining protein semi-synthesis with electrophysiology, biochemistry, fluorometry and molecular dynamics simulations, we control phosphorylation at Y1495 in the DIII-DIV linker and demonstrate how it governs regulation by intracellular fibroblast growth factor homologous factors (iFGFs). We find that iFGFs act through two separable mechanisms: a depolarizing SSI shift of around 16 mV that is switched off by phosphorylation, and a suppression of late current that proceeds regardless of phosphorylation. Only the former requires an intact C-terminal domain/DIII-DIV linker interaction, and both differ between iFGF isoforms. Phosphorylation at Y1495 therefore does not switch off the iFGF interaction but instead redirects its output. Together, this reveals a mode of ion channel regulation in which a single post-translational modification selects between different functional consequences of a protein-protein interaction.

title: Extending Axiomatic Design: A Dual-Domain Mapping Framework for Complete Physical Architecture — Co-Generating Functional and Decoupling Components
abstract: This paper extends Axiomatic Design (AD) to address a fundamental design problem in physical architecture synthesis: functional-centric mapping fails to characterize physical field coupling, and decoupling components lack representation within the existing framework. The core scientific question is: Does functional independence imply physical independence? If not, what representational extensions are required for function-centric design theory to characterize physical field coupling and enabling the systematic recommendation of decoupling components?

title: Click-Functionalizable Tetrathiafulvalene-Tetrathiolate Diradicaloids as Modular NIR-II Fluorophores
abstract: Near-infrared (NIR) emissive fluorophores are appealing for biological imaging and sensing applications, particularly in the lower-energy NIR-II region (1000–1700 nm). Compared to light in the visible and NIR-I regions, NIR-II light undergoes less absorption and scattering by biological tissues, enabling deeper tissue penetration and higher imaging resolution. Tetrathiafulvalene-tetrathiolate (TTFtt)-bridged bimetallic diradicaloid complexes exhibit bright NIR-II emission with high photoluminescence quantum yields (PLQYs) relative to other NIR-II fluorophores.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Key molecules, diagnostic models and immune microenvironment analysis of ischemic stroke based on pyroptosis and immunosuppression-related genes
abstract: Ischemic Stroke (IS) represents a significant global health challenge due to its high morbidity and mortality rates, necessitating an urgent need for enhanced diagnostic and therapeutic strategies. The present study aimed to construct a multi-gene diagnostic model for IS while elucidating the underlying molecular mechanisms and identifying critical genes associated with pyroptosis and immune suppression.

title: Unraveling bonding evolution in carbon-centered gold(I) clusters
abstract: Gold nanoclusters, composed of a small number of gold atoms, can exhibit optical, electronic and catalytic properties distinct from those of bulk gold. One intriguing family consists of carbon-centered gold(I) clusters, in which a carbon atom is surrounded by several gold atoms. Unlike the familiar four-coordinate carbon in methane, the central carbon in these clusters can be coordinated by five or even six gold atoms.

title: Macrocycle 2D COF Single Crystal
abstract: We report the synthesis of a two-dimensional (2D) covalent organic framework (COF) single crystal, termed COF-900, constructed from a geminiarene-type macrocycle linker, biphenyl-extended pillar[3]arene containing nine phenyl units. The atomically accurate structure was resolved by three-dimensional electron diffraction (3D ED) of the 2D COF single crystal with a resolution of 1.2 Å, unveiling the conformation of the macrocycle in the layered backbone as well as AB interlayer stacking.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: A Lightweight Log-Mel CNN for Audio Deepfake Detection: An Empirical Study of Speaker-Disjoint and Cross-Dataset Generalization
abstract: Synthetic speech generated by text-to-speech and voice-conversion systems can be difficult to distinguish from bonafide speech, creating a need for practical audio-spoofing detectors. This report describes a compact convolutional neural network (CNN) that classifies audio as real or fake using log-Mel spectrogram features. The supplied implementation combines the ASVspoof 2019 Logical Access training partition with the training partition of the In-the-Wild dataset.

title: Molecular Origins of Negative Catalysis in Synthetic CO2 Fixation Cycles
abstract: Crotonyl-CoA carboxylase/reductase (Ccr) is among the fastest known CO2-fixing enzymes and is a key catalyst in the design of synthetic CO2 fixation pathways. Ccr catalyzes the reductive carboxylation of enoyl-CoA esters via a reactive enolate intermediate to build the products after CO2 addition. In the absence of CO2, the enolate can be covalently trapped transiently as a noninhibitory C2 adduct, which enhances the catalytic efficiency of carboxylation by suppressing competing side reactions.

title: Precision in Predicting Catalytic Performance of Medium Chain Dehydrogenase: A Benchmark Data Set and Comparative Metrics
abstract: Medium-chain dehydrogenases/reductases are highly versatile oxidoreductases with broad industrial relevance but complex structure-function relationships that continue to challenge catalytic performance prediction. A Benchmark for Medium-Chain Dehydrogenases (MCDBench) is introduced as a rigorously curated benchmark dataset comprising 792 enzyme-substrate-cofactor combinations, including experimentally validated inactive cases obtained under standardized conditions. MCDBench spans 36 chemically diverse alcohol substrates, representative MDR subclasses, and multiple cofactor types, enabling systematic evaluation of model generalization. Benchmarking four representative activity-prediction models (DLKcat, UniKP, TurNuP, and CataPro) shows that correlations with experimental activities remain modest under standardized conditions, and that distinguishing active from inactive catalytic space remains a practical challenge across enzyme classes and substrate types. Analysis points to a positive-data skew inherited from widely used biochemical databases and the relative scarcity of validated negative samples as key factors shaping this behavior. By providing a standardized benchmark that integrates experimentally validated negative cases, MCDBench offers a unified experimental and computational framework to help the field measure and further improve the discrimination of active and inactive catalytic space for biocatalyst design.

title: SMSTPred: Protein Language Model Embeddings Predict SAM-Methyltransferase Substrate Specificity and Reveal Metabolite Methyltransferasome Enrichment in Plants and Actinomycetota
abstract: S-adenosyl-methionine (SAM)-dependent methyltransferases (MTases) are one of the largest and most ancient enzyme superfamilies in biology, transferring a methyl group from SAM to substrates as different as DNA, RNA, proteins, and small-molecule metabolites. Most SAM-MTases share a Class I Rossmann-like SAM-binding core, with substrate specificity determined by variable inserts and accessory domains rather than the conserved fold; as a result, substrate type is unknown for most MTases in sequence databases, which are dominated by unreviewed entries. Here we present SMSTPred (SAM-Methyltransferase Substrate-Type Predictor), a multi-label classifier that predicts MTase substrate type from protein language model embeddings and benchmarks it under homology-disjoint cross-validation against sequence-homology, structure-homology, and profile-HMM baselines. SMSTPred reaches a cluster-disjoint Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) of 0.94, significantly ahead of sequence-homology (MMseqs2, 0.85), structure-homology (Foldseek, 0.89) and profile-HMM (0.52) baselines, while providing calibrated, per-substrate confidence. Applying it to ~116,000 MTases across 1,249 reference proteomes, we map the substrate landscape of methylation across the tree of life. Substrate specialization tracks taxonomy: animals expand protein- and DNA-methylation, whereas small-molecule methyltransferases are enriched in plants and Actinomycetota; in Actinomycetota beyond what is expected for their proteome size, and in plants in proportion to their larger proteomes. The predictions identify thousands of uncharacterized methyltransferases with substrate type assignments (about half of those in uncharacterized clusters), many corroborated by an independent reaction-retrieval method. Notably, ~11% of enzymes with a single substrate call lack any class-discriminative sequence motif, suggesting that substrate specificity is often encoded beyond short linear motifs. Together, this work provides SMSTPred, a substrate-type predictor for Class I methyltransferases, and a tree-of-life resource of testable functional hypotheses.

title: Tetrapeptide caspase inhibitors exhibit protease- and substrate-dependent off-target specificity
abstract: Peptide-based caspase inhibitors are widely used to define the functions of individual caspases and were developed from tetrapeptide substrate preferences identified using positional scanning peptide libraries. Their specificity is typically validated using fluorogenic tetrapeptide substrates, yet whether these assays accurately predict inhibition of endogenous protein substrates has not been systematically examined. Here, we demonstrate that the widely used executioner caspase inhibitor zDEVD-FMK directly inhibits caspase-1 (CASP1)-mediated processing of interleukin-1{beta} (IL-1{beta}) and interleukin-18 (IL-18) despite CASP1 exhibiting minimal activity toward the DEVD fluorogenic substrate. Unexpectedly, zDEVD-FMK selectively inhibited CASP1 but not the closely related inflammatory caspases CASP4 or CASP5. Conversely, the CASP1 inhibitor Ac-YVAD-CMK directly inhibited CASP3-mediated protein substrate cleavage. We further found that endogenous substrates displayed markedly different sensitivities to inhibition, with IL-1{beta} and IL-18 processing consistently inhibited more efficiently than gasdermin D cleavage, while fluorogenic CASP3/7 reporter cleavage substantially overestimated inhibition of endogenous apoptotic substrates. During inflammasome activation and Salmonella infection, DEVD- and YVAD-based inhibitors failed to distinguish apoptotic executioner caspase activity from inflammatory caspase signaling. Together, our findings demonstrate that fluorogenic tetrapeptide assays do not faithfully predict inhibition of endogenous protein substrates and identify protease- and substrate-dependent specificity as fundamental features of peptide-based caspase inhibitors.

title: Repurposing a biosynthetic enzyme for imaging UDP-glucose dynamics in living systems
abstract: Metabolite dynamics remain difficult to visualize in living systems, particularly for nucleotide sugars that link metabolism to glycosylation and signaling. Here we repurpose Helicobacter pylori UDP-glucose pyrophosphorylase to develop UGluS, a genetically encoded ratiometric fluorescent sensor for its biosynthetic product, UDP-glucose (UDP-Glc). Circularly permuted GFP insertion and directed evolution yield an approximately 18-fold excitation-ratio response and an apparent dissociation constant of 32.5 M, with preferential responsiveness to UDP-Glc over related metabolites. Live-cell imaging and microplate assays reveal responses to metabolic, genetic and mechanosensitive perturbations in mammalian cells. In zebrafish larvae, UGluS reveals uridine-induced increases in UDP-Glc availability and fin-fold enrichment. In mouse liver slices and skeletal muscle in vivo, insulin- and glucose-induced decreases in UDP-Glc availability accompany increased glycogen content. These findings establish UGluS as a tool for imaging UDP-Glc dynamics across biological scales and extend the use of biosynthetic enzymes as fluorescent sensing scaffolds.

title: Striking Differences in Tetrabromobisphenol A (TBBPA) Deconjugation by Human Fecal Microbiota: The Pilot-10 Human Donor Study
abstract: Tetrabromobisphenol A (TBBPA) is a widely used brominated flame retardant with multiple adverse health effects. Although TBBPA undergoes phase II conjugation to facilitate elimination, gut microbial deconjugation may regenerate unconjugated TBBPA, increasing intestinal re-exposure. However, the extent of interindividual variability and its underlying microbial determinants remain poorly understood. To address this critical knowledge gap, we hypothesized that human fecal microbiota exhibit donor-dependent differences in TBBPA-sulfate (S-TBBPA) deconjugation and potential downstream debromination to tribromobisphenol A (Tri-BBPA). In our Pilot-10 Human Donor Study (PM10), fecal microbiota from five healthy adult male and five female human donors were incubated anaerobically with S-TBBPA at 37 C for six hours. Heat-inactivated microbiota served as controls. S-TBBPA, unconjugated TBBPA, and Tri-BBPA were quantified using targeted liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS). Metagenomic shotgun sequencing (MGS) was performed followed by microbial taxonomic and gene-family profiling using MetaPhlAn v4.11 and HUMAnN v3.9, respectively. Unheated fecal microbiota from all donors regenerated TBBPA, whereas heat inactivation nearly abolished its formation, supporting microbial enzyme-dependent deconjugation of S-TBBPA. The proportion of regenerated TBBPA varied substantially among donors, accounting for approximately 10-50% of the combined detected S-TBBPA and TBBPA. No statistically significant sex-associated differences were detected. Tri-BBPA was undetectable or negligible across incubations. Notably, the cumulative sulfatase-maturation enzyme gene family abundance was positively associated with LC-MS-measured S-TBBPA deconjugation activity, whereas the cumulative arylsulfatase and other sulfatase gene abundances showed no significant associations. Furthermore, 12 taxonomically stratified microbial desulfation-related gene-family annotations exhibited nominally significant positive correlations with deconjugation activity, highlighting potential roles for specific microbial sulfatases and their maturation enzymes in TBBPA reactivation. Collectively, our PM10 pilot study revealed substantial interindividual variability in microbial TBBPA-sulfate deconjugation and identified sulfatase-maturation enzyme gene abundance as a potential indicator of activity. These findings highlighted an underexplored pathway of xenobiotic reactivation and support future personalized microbiome-directed strategies to reduce internal TBBPA exposure and associated health risks.

title: Elucidating the Sodium Channel-Targeting Anti-Seizure Medication Interactome: A Drug-Target Pathway Analysis
abstract: Epilepsy is a common neurological disorder in both children and adults, primarily managed with anti-seizure medications (ASMs). Sodium channel blockers are among the most commonly used ASMs. These medications exhibit distinct spectra of efficacy and side effect profiles. These likely result from different off-target interactions, protein binding profiles, and subunit selectivity that remain poorly characterized. We developed a neural network-based computational pipeline to systematically elucidate the molecular targets and associated biological pathways of selected sodium channel-modulating ASMs: carbamazepine, lamotrigine, eslicarbazepine, licarbazepine, lacosamide, phenytoin, and cenobamate. Using the DRIFT (Drug-target identification based on chemical similarity) algorithm for proteome-wide target prediction, we identified protein targets for these ASMs. The sodium channel alpha subunit family was the highest-ranked target for every drug except cenobamate, for which it ranked second behind the GABA-A receptor. Pathway mapping in the Reactome database revealed both shared and drug-specific biological processes. Furthermore, molecular docking studies elucidated the atomistic interactions between the drugs and the predicted targets. Specifically, the predicted target landscape varied from eslicarbazepine and licarbazepine (59 predicted targets each) to lacosamide (18). Pathway analysis revealed recurrent enrichment in rapid depolarisation and the interaction between L1 and ankyrins shared across all drugs, alongside predicted off-targets, including the cannabinoid CB1 receptor for phenytoin and the carbonic anhydrases for lacosamide. Molecular docking supported these predictions, with binding scores ranging from -24 to -31 kcal/mol. Overall, this work provides a systems-level view of NaV-targeting ASM pharmacology and a hypothesis-generating framework to prioritize mechanistic and combination studies of these medications in epilepsy.

title: Amperometric reconstruction favors a toroidal fusion pore during kiss-and-run release of serotonin
abstract: Kiss-and-run amperometric currents reveal the opening and closing cycle of the fusion pore. This study uses such information along with mathematical approaches to test whether the pore is toroidal or cylindrical. Individual kiss-and-run amperometric currents from serotonin release by leech Retzius neurons were used to reconstruct either a toroid of fixed rim curvature or a cylinder of fixed length.

title: Molecular simulation of ion-mediated phase separation and structural organization in RNA condensates
abstract: Phase separation of RNA is strongly influenced by ions, yet the molecular mechanisms by which ion-RNA interactions affect RNA condensation and internal organization remain poorly understood. Here, we use coarse-grained molecular simulations to investigate how temperature, ions and RNA sequence collectively regulate condensate formation and organization. We find that RNA condensates selectively enrich Mg2+ through dynamic multidentate phosphate coordination, producing ion concentrations several orders of magnitude higher than in surrounding solution. Rather than creating a uniform dense phase, this ion enrichment establishes spatial gradients in ion-RNA interactions that generate distinct microenvironments in the condensate. RNAs in the condensate core accumulate more Mg2+, exhibit enhanced base stacking and transient helicity. These heterogeneous ionic environments emerge spontaneously even in condensates composed of a single RNA species and are further modulated by RNA sequence through differences in Mg2+ binding and packing in condensate. Together, our simulations provide a molecular-level framework for understanding the origins of heterogeneous organization in ion-mediated RNA condensates.

title: Editorial: GLP-1s and the limits of postnormal science
abstract: The hype and promise of these drugs reflect the challenge of inclusive problem-solving when the stakes are high

title: Glass casings skew electrochemical measurements
abstract: Insulating tubes around reference electrodes can create signals that researchers could mistake for real electrode processes

title: Reaction-Dependent Predictability of Yields from Small Substrate-Scope Datasets
abstract: We evaluate structure-based regression using molecular fingerprints and ElasticNet across four reaction datasets (96–190 reactions). The models outperform constant-yield baselines for two transformations, including literature-assembled umpolung amide synthesis. Learning curves reveal reaction-dependent data requirements, with useful predictions emerging from 20 training examples in favorable cases.

title: Atomic Layer Ordering of 2D van der Waals Ion Channels Enables Ultrathin and Highly Selective Membranes
abstract: Developing ultrathin, highly selective membranes that emulate biological ion channels is a primary goal of synthetic membrane technology. Although two-dimensional (2D) materials offer a promising platform for constructing subnanometer fluidic channels, simultaneously achieving high permeance and excellent selectivity in 2D ionic membranes remains a significant challenge. This bottleneck originates from the complexities involved in controlling the precise structural arrangement within nanosheet assemblies. In this work, we demonstrate that the atomic-layer ordering of 2D van der Waals (vdW) ion channels is a decisive factor in achieving ultrathin, highly selective membranes. By assembling 2D titania nanosheets with atomic layer-by-layer regularity, we fabricate atomic stacking membranes (ASMs) that achieve near-unity ion selectivity within an ultrathin (∼50 nm) framework. The structural regularity of these ASMs causes continuous overlap of the electrical double layer throughout the 2D ion channels, facilitating robust electrostatic regulation and maximizing selectivity. The result is further confirmed by transmission electron microscopy, grazing-incidence wide-angle X-ray scattering analysis, and molecular dynamics simulations. Leveraging the “Lego-like” modular assembly advantage of ASMs, we demonstrate multifunctional heterostructural iontronic devices and gate-controlled iontronic transistors featuring on/off ratios up to 104. Furthermore, the well-ordered 2D ion channels within these ASMs enable high-performance osmotic energy harvesting. This solution-processable atomic-layer van der Waals assembly strategy for ultrathin and highly selective ASMs establishes a versatile platform for uniformly regulating 2D angstrom-scale ion transport, paving the way for advanced biomimetic iontronics and efficient energy conversion.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: IMPRESS: AI-coupled HPC workflows for protein design
abstract: Protein design campaigns are often run as multi-stage pipelines with a generative backbone model, an inverse-folding model, and a structure predictor chained together in that order. The stages differ by one to two orders of magnitude in cost per candidate, and the allocation of sampling effort across them is fixed before a campaign begins. Such a filter cascade can only discard candidates. It cannot redirect sampling toward the regions of design space a model stack can reach, and for targets whose constraints are far from the generative model's training distribution it may return no solution at any practical sample count. We present IMPRESS (Integrated Machine-learning for PRotein Structures at Scale), a framework in which design pipelines are stateful objects that halt, continue, resample, or branch at runtime from their own accumulated results. Adaptive decisions are evaluated asynchronously with respect to execution, so a campaign refines itself without global synchronization. We apply IMPRESS to three problems: backbone generation on discontinuous enzyme active-site motifs, de novo small molecule binder design, and PDZ binder redesign. Adaptive parameterization solves active-site motifs carried on three or more discontinuous residue islands that a fixed cascade does not solve, shifts the realized task mix toward inexpensive sequence exploration, and produces sequence ensembles that explore broadly but stay near their inputs. All comparisons reported here are between in silico metrics. We expect that adaptive parameterization will matter most for targets furthest from the training distributions of the underlying models, and that the same primitives will accommodate experimental measurement as a steering signal.

title: MolMap resolves functional chromatin responses to small-molecule perturbation
abstract: Small molecules can alter chromatin through protein-, DNA- and physicochemical interactions, yet current approaches do not directly resolve where these perturbations produce an immediate functional chromatin response in native nuclear environments. Here we present MolMap (chromatin-small Molecule Mapping), a sequencing-based method that profiles genome-wide chromatin responses to chemically unmodified compounds in isolated, non-crosslinked nuclei. Rather than measuring ligand binding, protein occupancy or downstream gene expression, MolMap identifies genomic regions where small-molecule exposure produces an immediate functional chromatin response. By quantifying changes in Tn5 accessibility and local chromatin organization in native nuclei, MolMap captures locus-specific and dose-dependent effects while separating early chromatin responses from downstream cellular adaptation. Across metabolites, protein-targeting compounds, a DNA-binding drug and a physicochemical chromatin modulator, MolMap resolved compound-specific and mechanistically distinct responses. Comparison with live-cell ATAC-seq showed that MolMap captures early chromatin responses before broader cellular adaptation. In leukemia models, MolMap revealed a coordinated chromatin response in drug-sensitive cells that was strongly attenuated in resistant models. MolMap therefore provides a native framework for bridging the precision of biochemical perturbation assays with the breadth of genome-wide profiling, extending classical chromatin biochemistry into a genomic setting.

title: A Wrong Ground-State Structure of HfO2 Predicted by Machine-Learning Interatomic Potentials Based on the Perdew−Burke−Ernzerhof Functional
abstract: Machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) have become powerful tools for material simulations. Many MLIPs are trained based on density functional theory (DFT) datasets generated with the Perdew−Burke−Ernzerhof (PBE) exchange−correlation functional. Using a PBE-based MLIP for HfO2, we identify a low-energy I41/amd structure, which is predicted to be more stable than the well-known ground-state structure, the monoclinic P21/c structure. Since experiments show clearly that HfO2 takes the P21/c structure as the ground state, this is obviously a wrong prediction.

title: Evolution-Guided Engineering of a Process-Compatible Thymidine Phosphorylase for the Scalable Cascade Biosynthesis of 2′/3′-Functionalized Purine Nucleoside Analogs
abstract: 2′/3′-Functionalized nucleoside analogs are valuable therapeutic agents and essential building blocks for nucleic acid-based medicines; however, their scalable biocatalytic synthesis remains challenging due to insufficient enzyme robustness under process-relevant conditions. Here, we developed an ancestral sequence reconstruction (ASR)-guided engineering strategy integrated with kcat/Km-based virtual screening to generate a process-compatible thymidine phosphorylase (TP) variant for scalable nucleoside biosynthesis.

title: Machine learning-guided discovery of TMX4@G electrocatalysts with LLM-assisted workflow automation
abstract: Coordination-engineered transition-metal single-atom catalysts offer a modular platform for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), but their discovery is hindered by the large configurational space arising from coupled metal-ligand variations. Here we develop a symmetry-aware and uncertainty-guided workflow to accelerate the screening of TMX4@G catalysts (X = C, N, O, P or S), where a transition-metal atom is coordinated by four ligands embedded in graphene.

title: Charge-transfer excitation drives cooperative phonon-assisted exciton self-trapping in NiPS$_3$
abstract: Carrier self-trapping is a fundamental relaxation pathway in strongly correlated quantum materials, yet the microscopic lattice motions that drive it have remained largely inaccessible to direct observation. Here we investigate the van der Waals antiferromagnet NiPS$_3$ upon excitation across its ligand-to-metal charge-transfer gap, and reveal a nonequilibrium pathway that initially generates unbound carriers before they evolve into correlated excitonic states. Using ultrabroadband optical-pump terahertz-probe spectroscopy, we simultaneously track carrier localization and the associated lattice dynamics in real time. The transient conductive response quenches with a time constant of $\sim$109 fs and evolves into a localized exciton state, accompanied by pronounced renormalization of Ni-S optical phonons and the emergence of a transient 2.7 THz vibrational mode. Temperature-dependent measurements, together with mode-resolved dielectric dynamics and symmetry analysis, identify the 2.7 and 8.0 THz responses as spectroscopic indicators of exciton self-trapping and point to a cooperative two-phonon mechanism. These findings establish the excitation pathway as a key parameter controlling carrier localization and many-body relaxation in strongly coupled quantum materials.

title: Dynamics of a Single-Domain Dissipative Magnetic Gyroscope in Electric and Magnetic Fields
abstract: We formulate the coupled spin--rotation dynamics of a single-domain symmetric top ferromagnetic needle (a magnetic gyroscope) in static magnetic and electric fields. The conservative Hamiltonian contains the rotational kinetic energy, the magnetocrystalline and shape anisotropy, the Zeeman energy, the electrostatic energy of the dipole induced in the conducting needle, the linear magnetoelectric coupling, and the relativistic motional (spin-orbit) coupling. Gilbert damping is introduced, and in an electric field, Debye relaxation of the induced electric dipole of the conducting needle also results in dissipation. We give the equations of motion in the laboratory and body-fixed frames, with singularity-free quaternion kinematics. For a 120-nm-long single-domain cobalt needle in a 0.5~T field we find: (i) because the anisotropy field ($\approx 1.3$~T) exceeds the applied magnetic field, the spin reverses direction several times during the initial Gilbert-damping transient, and the parity of the number of reversals determines whether the easy axis ends up parallel or antiparallel to the spin; (ii) after the transient the needle librates about the field---precession accompanied by nutation at twice the precession frequency---with a period of about 20~ns, consistent with the libration period $2π(I_1/μB)^{1/2}$, while the Zeeman and rotational kinetic energies oscillate out of phase and the total energy is conserved; (iii) a static electric field $\mathbf E$ exerts on the conducting needle a shape-dependent polarization torque that tends to align the long axis of the needle with $\mathbf E$. The torques due to the magnetoelectric interaction and motional magnetic fields ($\lesssim1~μ$T) are negligible compared with the polarization torque. A conducting needle can therefore serve as a magnetometer only if $E\ll E_c$.

title: Localized corrosion resistance of ultrafine-grained austenitic steel 321 obtained by Rotary Swaging: The role of annealing conditions
abstract: The object of this study was austenitic steel 321, which has an ultrafine-grained (UFG) structure formed by Rotary Swaging (RS). RS leads to the formation of a two-phase macroscopically heterogeneous and, at the same time, a microscopically homogeneous UFG structure with an increased content of martensite. It has been shown that secondary TiC nanoparticles form in the annealing at 450-550C, the reverse transformation of martensite into austenite occurs at 550-650C, and recrystallization begins at 700C. Electrochemical studies of the resistance of the UFG steel to general corrosion, intergranular corrosion (IGC), and pitting corrosion (PC) have been carried out. It has been shown that the UFG steel after RS has a reduced IGC resistance. The surface of steel rods after RS has a reduced hardness and corrosion resistance compared to the central part of the rods. It has been shown that in the temperature range of 450-550C, there is a slight increase in the microhardness, and a significant decrease in the IGC and PC resistance of the UFG steel. Recrystallization at 700-800C leads to an increased PC resistance and IGC resistance. Annealing conditions have been determined that ensure a good combination of strength, ductility and corrosion resistance of the UFG steel. It was demonstrated that to explain the non-monotonic variation in the localized corrosion rate of UFG steel during annealing, it is necessary to consider not only the well-known effects of martensite and delta-ferrite, but also the precipitation of TiC particles and the changes in the free energy of non-equilibrium grain boundaries.

title: Second-Order Polarization Propagator Approximation to the Quadratic Unitary Coupled Cluster Framework I: First-Order Properties
abstract: We have developed a new formulation for calculating first-order properties in the quadratic unitary coupled-cluster singles and doubles (qUCCSD) method, using a second-order polarizable propagator approximation. The accuracy and reliability of this new framework of the proposed approach have been assessed through the calculation of ground- and excited-state dipole moments and oscillator strengths for a set of small molecules. The Hermiticity of the UCC similarity-transformed Hamiltonian allows molecular properties to be evaluated without introducing left-hand eigenvectors, thereby simplifying the theoretical formulation and computational procedure. Furthermore, the proposed formulation preserves the size-intensivity of transition moments, a property that is not generally guaranteed within the conventional non-Hermitian equation-of-motion coupled-cluster framework. To assess the performance of the proposed method, we have benchmarked both ground- and excited-state properties for 11 small molecules against the extrapolated full configuration interaction (exFCI) reference values and compared with the conventional coupled cluster singles and doubles (CCSD) and third-order algebraic diagrammatic construction (ADC(3)) results. The qUCCSD method yields average errors comparable to those of CCSD while demonstrating significantly improved accuracy over the ADC(3) method.

title: The MC-QTAIM: Why, How, and When?
abstract: The multi-component quantum theory of atoms in molecules (MC-QTAIM) generalizes the original QTAIM framework developed by Richard Bader and colleagues, extending atoms-in-molecules analysis beyond ab initio electronic wavefunctions. MC-QTAIM facilitates the examination of the AIM structure in systems and states that require MC wavefunctions, which describe systems containing multiple distinguishable classes of quantum particles. This advancement broadens the applicability of AIM analysis to a wide range of quantum systems and states that were previously inaccessible. These include exotic molecules, such as positronic species; exotic quantum states, such as superposed proton states in molecules with two- or multi-well potential energy surfaces; and non-adiabatic states of conventional molecules. In this review, I aim to explain the fundamental principles of MC-QTAIM analysis in accessible language and explore some of its potential applications. Additionally, the general formalism for energy partitioning in MC systems, called MC Interacting Quantum Atoms (MC-IQA), is introduced. This scheme unifies the energy partitioning of numerous quantum systems and encompasses the IQA method originally developed by Pendas and colleagues, as well as the previously developed two-component IQA (TC-IQA) scheme - developed by our group to analyze positronic systems - as special cases.

title: Effect of superplastic deformation on the intergranular corrosion resistance of austenitic steel 321 with different types of UFG structure: A case of homogeneous and heterogeneous microstructure obtained by ECAP
abstract: The effects of superplasticity (SP) on the structure, hardness, and intergranular corrosion (IGC) resistance of UFG 321L steel are reported. By increasing the number of the ECAP cycles (N) and varying the ECAP temperature, and annealing temperature, the degree of the microstructural heterogeneity was changed. Regardless of the microstructural homogeneity degree, UFG steels demonstrated the possibility of realizing the SP effect at temperatures below the onset temperature of dynamic recrystallization. The dependence of ductility of the UFG steel on the test temperature is non-monotonic with a minimum at 450-600C. The maximum elongation to failure (~250%) was achieved at a SP temperature of 800C. The SP deformation of the UFG steel is controlled by the power law creep. It is shown that the hardness of UFG steel samples after SP is equal than the hardness of UFG steels annealed at the same temperature. It is also shown what SP leads to a decrease in the IGC resistance of the UFG steel. Heterostructured steel have reduced ductility, as well as lower resistance to IGC after tension tests at room temperature (RT). The minimum IGC resistance is ensured at N=2, and the maximum - at N=4. The IGC resistance of homogeneous UFG samples after tension testing exceeds the IGC resistance of coarse-grained steel. Tension test at a RT has the greatest negative effect on the IGC resistance of heterostructured steel, and the least negative effect on the IGC resistance of homogeneous steel. Increasing the number of ECAP cycles enhances the ductility of the UFG steel at 750-900C. Increasing the ECAP temperature results in a simultaneous decrease in ductility and flow stress. Heterostructured steel exhibits minimal values of the activation energy of SP deformation. Increasing the number of ECAP cycles and increasing the ECAP temperature lead to an increase in the activation energy of SP deformation.

title: CircDNA-PAINT: high-resolution binary-barcode multiplexing with circular DNA docking strands
abstract: Understanding key biological processes governed by cell surface protein distribution requires highly multiplexed imaging. Binary barcode methods based on DNA hybridization represent a powerful approach to such imaging; however, higher multiplexing demands longer DNA barcodes, which substantially compromise localization resolution. Here we introduce circular DNA-based multiplexed DNA-PAINT (CircDNA-PAINT), a method that achieves a resolution better than 20 nm and thus enables robust binary encoded multiplexing. This approach avoids the linear time overhead of adaptor-cycling DNA-PAINT and greatly shortens acquisition time for large-plex imaging. CircDNA-PAINT provides a new tool for dissecting complex nanoscale cellular architectures.

title: Single-Molecule Fluorescence Imaging Reveals the Kinetic Origin of Wettability-Controlled Photocatalytic Selectivity
abstract: Interfacial wettability strongly influences photocatalytic selectivity, but the kinetic origin of this effect remains unclear. Although adsorption differences and dominant reactive oxygen species (ROS) pathways are often invoked to explain wettability-dependent selectivity, neither fully reveals how interfacial reaction environments determine catalytic outcomes.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Diastereoselective Alkylation of Tryptophan and Tryptophan-Containing Peptides via Cooperative Rh(II)/Chiral Phosphoric Acid Catalysis
abstract: A cooperative Rh(II)/chiral phosphoric acid (CPA) catalytic system enables highly diastereoselective alkylation of tryptophan derivatives and Trp-containing peptides at both the N(1) and C(6) positions. The reaction exhibits substrate-controlled regioselectivity: unmodified tryptophan derivatives undergo N(1)-alkylation, whereas preinstallation of a phenyl directing group at C(2) switches the selectivity to C(6)-alkylation, with both modes proceeding with high stereocontrol (up to 99:1 dr).

title: Residue-Specific Determinants of CO2 Reduction in a Tungsten-Containing Formate Dehydrogenase
abstract: Metal-dependent formate dehydrogenases catalyze the reversible interconversion of CO2 and formate with high efficiency, yet their catalytic mechanism remains the subject of active debate, highlighting the need for studies that better define the role of individual residues. Previous mutational studies have focused mainly on formate oxidation, while the contribution of specific residues to CO2 reduction remains poorly understood.

title: Hidden topological signatures in a van der Waals ferromagnet revealed by spin-resolved circular-dichroic photoemission
abstract: Layered ferromagnets with strongly correlated electrons provide a platform for exploring the interplay among magnetism, spin-orbit coupling, and nontrivial band topology. $\mathrm{Ni}_{1/4}\mathrm{TaSe}_2$ is a correlated van der Waals ferromagnet with a transition temperature of 58 K that lies close in composition to a superconducting phase that emerges upon Ni depletion. Here, we combine spin- and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, circular-dichroism measurements, and density functional theory calculations to investigate its spin-resolved electronic structure. We observe spin-polarized states crossing the Fermi level and signatures of broken time-reversal symmetry in the ferromagnetic state. Spin-resolved circular-dichroism measurements further reveal a helicity-dependent spin response consistent with a finite spin Berry curvature and suggestive of local topological character. Together, these results establish an experimental connection between ferromagnetism, spin-polarized electronic states, and topological signatures in $\mathrm{Ni}_{1/4}\mathrm{TaSe}_2$, providing a foundation for investigating how these properties may relate to the emergence of superconductivity upon Ni depletion.

title: AlCoCuFeNi High-Entropy Alloy Nanoparticle Melting and Solidification: A Classical Molecular Dynamics Simulation Study
abstract: The processes of melting and solidification of an AlCoCuFeNi high-entropy alloy nanoparticle with a diameter of about 10 nm were studied by classical molecular dynamics simulation using an embedded atom model potential. Three cooling rates, 10^11, 10^12, and 10^13 K/s, were considered. Melting and crystallization behavior were characterized through the temperature dependence of the potential energy. Structural evolution was analyzed using adaptive common-neighbor analysis (CNA) and radial distribution functions (RDF). The results show that the final structure changes from amorphous to crystalline as the cooling rate decreases. A pronounced temperature hysteresis associated with melting and crystallization was also observed.

title: Super-resolved mass photometry reveals the dissociation pathways of individual protein complexes
abstract: Mass photometry (MP) measures the mass of single unlabelled molecules as they adsorb to a glass surface, but conventional analysis captures each molecule only momentarily, as it binds, and neglects its subsequent fate. Here we correct for coverslip drift and use mass-dependent localisation precision to link successive events at one site to a single molecule and enables two workflows for studying protein assemblies. In tandem MP, matching each binding event with its outcomes yields a two-dimensional precursor-product spectrum that separates dissociation from unbinding, providing structural insights into the protein assemblies and the kinetics of subunit loss. By comparing citrate synthase homologues, we reveal distinct fingerprints and disassembly pathways among complexes of the same oligomeric state. In particle tracking, differential imaging allows for continuous recording of particle mass and position. By examining adeno-associated virus capsids, we recovered accurate masses, and reveals acid-induced disassembly and movement behaviour that depends on both viral and imaging surfaces. Our code is freely available and applies to data obtained on commercial instruments with minimal changes to experimental protocols, offering additional dimensions to MP analysis beyond the mass histogram to return time-resolved, single-molecule histories.

title: Integrated Multi-Omics and Machine Learning for Prioritizing Candidate Plasma Proteins in Alzheimer's Disease and Predicting Multi-Target Interactions of Traditional Chinese Medicine
abstract: This study integrated multi-omics data and machine learning to prioritize candidate plasma proteins and to predict the multi-target interactions of traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) in Alzheimer's disease (AD). Mendelian randomization across three cohorts (Icelandic, UK Biobank, and Fenland) identified 66 AD-associated plasma proteins, including TREM2, ACE, GRN, and CR1, with TREM2 showing a robust protective effect (OR = 0.78, 95% CI: 0.75-0.81). Single-cell RNA sequencing showed neuron-specific downregulation of NSF and TMEM106B in AD, implicating synaptic dysfunction and impaired axonal transport. A machine-learning classifier (K-nearest neighbors, KNN) incorporating TREM2, TMEM106B, C1S, PLOD2, and NSF, trained on brain-tissue expression data, demonstrated moderate predictive performance (AUC = 0.76, 95% CI: 0.63-0.90) and is presented as a candidate brain-tissue-derived classifier rather than a validated non-invasive plasma diagnostic panel. Immune infiltration analysis revealed altered M2 macrophage and plasma cell dynamics, with NSF negatively correlated with γδ T-cell infiltration (p < 0.001). Network pharmacology prioritized five candidate TCM herbs (e.g., Scutellaria baicalensis [Huang Qin] and Alpinia oxyphylla [Yi Zhi]) and bioactive compounds (stigmasterol and quercetin) targeting AD-related proteins. Molecular docking predicted strong binding between stigmasterol and PLOD2 (binding energy: -11.2kcal/mol), suggesting a potential role in modulating extracellular matrix remodeling. These compounds were enriched in the PI3K-Akt and NF-κB pathways, consistent with the anti-inflammatory effects observed in TCM formulations such as GHYSJ. These findings link candidate biomarker discovery with the predicted multi-target interactions of TCM, providing hypotheses for future non-invasive diagnosis and precision therapy in AD.

title: Spatiotemporal CNN LSTM Based Multi Class Stability Assessment of Renewable Integrated Power Systems Using PMU Measurements
abstract: The increasing penetration of renewable energy resources and the resulting variability in power-system operating conditions have created significant challenges for reliable real-time stability monitoring and corrective control. Conventional stability assessment methods often require extensive computation and may not satisfy the low-latency requirements of Wide Area Monitoring Systems (WAMS).

title: Confidence-Based Materials Data Quality Assessment via Domain Knowledge and Graph-Structured Learning
abstract: The rapid development of materials machine learning relies on large-scale, heterogeneous datasets, yet model reliability is often compromised by imperfect data from diverse experiments, simulations, and database integration. Real-world materials databases may contain measurement errors, failed calculations, missing or duplicate records, and hidden violations of physicochemical constraints. Such problems are difficult to identify because corrupted samples may remain statistically plausible rather than appearing as explicit outliers. In this paper, we propose a confidence-based materials data quality assessment framework that integrates domain knowledge with graph-structured learning. Data quality is formulated as a continuous confidence estimation problem rather than a binary anomaly identification task, enabling sample-level assessment and historical-reference-based batch comparison. A nine-dimensional feature-quality prior and duplicate-aware sample initialization are calibrated using materials domain rules and statistical evidence. Confidence is further refined through sample-feature bipartite graph propagation and weakly supervised graph attention, while a Memory-GAT module provides historical reference scoring. Experiments on 23 ODDS benchmark datasets show that the generic module achieves an average AUC-ROC of 0.866. In five repeated mixed-contamination experiments on mp\_20, rule calibration improves HistGradientBoostingRegressor test $R^2$ from $0.538\pm0.008$ to $0.616\pm0.014$. Graph refinement increases average precision from $0.943\pm0.004$ to 0.953\pm0.004$, while the rule-calibrated configuration has the highest mean test $R^2$ among the evaluated screening configurations. Five repeated MACE subset experiments further show an increase in $R^2$ from $0.590\pm0.053$ to $0.880\pm0.027$ after rule-based screening.

title: Where the Tokens Go: Heat, Entropy and Error in Agentic Coding
abstract: Coding agents are billed by the token, yet software engineering says nothing about what a token actually buys. Here we introduce a theory of software thermodynamics. The theory draws analogues from classical and stochastic thermodynamics, extends them, and applies them to modern agentic coding. We count the tokens an agent generates as its cost and divide that cost into work and heat. The test suite acts as a software Maxwell's daemon that judges every coding change. We test the theory with an analogue of the experiments in which a single molecule is pulled open and let fold again: an agent makes a change to a repository (coding) and then undoes it (uncoding), many times over, and we count the tokens of every model call. The cycle returns the requested edits to where they began, with each direction started from a stored reference tree, and the spread of its cost over repeated cycles defines a software temperature, which rose with the sampling temperature of the model. About 80 per cent of the tokens of a successful run are generated in model calls that leave the requested change where it was, and we call these tokens heat. The free energy of a change, which we estimate by analogy with the equality of Jarzynski, is 14 to 22 per cent of the mean cost of a successful coding run. Coding costs 1.1 to 1.5 times as much as uncoding. The daemon is imperfect: the verdict of a test suite varies with its environment, and a suite that accepts a broken change has a cost in tokens. The practical implication of the proposed theory could be new tools for analysing and optimising coding agents through the lens of thermodynamics.

title: Rewriting Copper-Catalyzed ATRA Reactions through a Cu(II)/Cu(III) Pathway
abstract: Atom transfer radical addition (ATRA) reactions are typically mediated by photocatalytic Cu(I)/Cu(II) redox cycles, whereas Cu(II) complexes generally serve as precursors to the catalytically active Cu(I) species. Herein, we report a Cu(II) complex supported by the rigid tridentate ligand 3,6-di-tert-butyl-1,8-di(pyridin-2-yl)-9H-carbazole (dpc) that displays an unexpected photocatalytic reactivity. While [Cu(dpc)OAc] exhibits low or no activity in established Cu(II)-mediated transformations, it efficiently catalyzes ATRA reactions, such as the chlorosulfonylation of alkenes, that are typical for Cu(I). Electrochemical and spectroscopic studies revealed that the rigid ligand framework suppresses conventional Cu(II)/Cu(I) photochemistry, instead enabling a Cu(II)/Cu(III) photocycle. Mechanistic investigations support the preassembly of a photoactive Cu(II)-sulfonyl chloride complex followed by light-induced radical generation and Cu(III)-mediated product formation. These findings establish a strategy for promoting ATRA reactivity through Cu(II)/Cu(III) catalysis and underline ligand design as a tool for controlling copper photochemistry.

title: Liquid-Phase Deep Carbon Elongation from C1 to Crystalline Graphite
abstract: Wet-chemical synthesis of well extended sp2-carbon from simple carbon feedstocks under mild solution-phase conditions remains a longstanding challenge due to the stringent requirements of reversible C–C coupling and error-correcting aromatization. Here, we show that a Lewis-acid-assisted triflic acid medium, TfOH/Hg(OTf)2, promotes the direct conversion of chloromethane solvents into condensed hydrocarbon products and even into crystalline graphitic flakes in a one-pot solution synthesis.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Stereochemical Identity of a Single Fluorosugar Enables Noninvasive Dual-Biomarker Fingerprinting of Cancer
abstract: Clinical molecular imaging of cancer largely relies on single biomarker-attributable readouts. Through an efficient trapping mechanism, 2-[18F]FDG robustly links PET readouts to the Warburg effect, illuminating only a single metabolic axis within the multichannel biochemical network of cancer. The versatile chemical space of synthetic fluorosugars, however, may offer an attractive framework for broadening the repertoire of metabolic markers accessible to noninvasive imaging. Here, we report Fluorine Metabolic Imaging (FMI), a molecular MRI strategy for simultaneous in vivo mapping of two metabolic biomarkers using a single probe. FMI exploits the altered biochemistry of 3-fluoro-3-deoxy-d-galactose (3FDGal), which undergoes orthogonal intracellular redox transformations mediated by ALDH1A1 and AKR1B1, each yielding a stably trapped fluorine-labeled metabolite with a characteristic 19F-NMR peak. Concurrently mapped by 19F-MRI, these two enzyme-attributable readouts enable noninvasive spatially resolved dual-biomarker visualization. We establish the trapping mechanism of 3FDGal and its enzymatic basis, demonstrating that 3FDGal-initiated fingerprints reflect dual-biomarker variations across different cancer cells. In vivo, FMI distinguishes tumors with contrasting metabolic phenotypes, herein demonstrated in human xenografts not detectable by the canonical 2-[18F]FDG-PET approach. Establishing this proof-of-concept platform for noninvasive multilayered tumor subtyping, FMI with fluorosugars extends metabolic imaging beyond the Warburg scheme into unexplored dimensions of cancer diagnostics.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Towards Cryogenic AI Hardware: Over 99% Precision In-Memory Computing at 4 K with 3-bit Ferroelectric Hf0.5Zr0.5O2 Capacitors
abstract: High-accuracy cryogenic hyperdimensional computing (HDC) is demonstrated using Hf0.5Zr0.5O2 (HZO) ferroelectric capacitors (FeCAPs) as multilevel analog memories for capacitive compute in-memory (CIM) architectures. On the ISOLET spoken-word dataset, FeCAP-stored vectors achieve up to 92% classification accuracy at 4 K, while charge-domain matrix-vector multiplication (MVM) exhibits near-ideal behaviour with linearity of 1 and error probability below 1% for 4x4 and 4x8 configurations, operating below 3 V. Unlike the performance at 300 K, HDC and CIM at 4 K remains resilient to electric-field-cycling-induced fatigue, thanks to enhanced cryogenic device characteristics, including reduced state variability, strongly suppressed leakage current and stable retention, as well as 78% faster switching. Furthermore, these multibit FeCAPs exhibit endurance beyond 1E9 cycles with polarization degradation below 8%, preserving multilevel integrity. Benefits can also be observed at 300 K, following cooldown and wake-up pulsing at 4 K and subsequent warming up. These results establish multibit FeCAPs as a highly reliable, ultra-low-energy, and accurate analog CIM platform for future cryogenic AI-computing hardware.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy and Navigation Behavior of Vision-Language Model Agents Reading Emergency CT and MRI Examinations
abstract: Purpose. To evaluate the diagnostic accuracy and image navigation behavior of vision-language model (VLM) agents under varying exploration strategies. Materials and Methods. In this retrospective study, six VLMs read 100 emergency CT and MRI examinations published in a public archive (March 2025-August 2026) under four conditions (free navigation, navigation from a key slice, and all slices or key slices in a single request), twice each (4800 runs). Nine radiologists read 30 of those cases. A large language model judge validated against two radiologists graded the answers. Conditions were compared with generalized estimating equations clustered by case. Results. Pooled accuracy was lowest under free navigation (32.6%; 391/1200), followed by navigation from a key slice (37.9%; 455/1200; P = .003), and highest with all slices (42.2%; 506/1200) or key slices (42.5%; 510/1200) in one request (both P < .001). On the 30 cases read by radiologists, freely navigating models were correct in 30.0% of runs (108/360) versus 77.0% for radiologists (208/270; P < .001). Models formed a first hypothesis after a median of 10.8% of the slices and kept it in 63.1% of runs (755/1196); final answers were correct in 12.4% of runs after a wrong first hypothesis (110/885) versus 90.4% after a right one (281/311; P < .001). Median stated confidence in the final answers was 90%, whereas 38.9% of them were correct (1861/4778). Conclusion. Across all exploration strategies, VLM agents remained far less accurate than radiologists. They adopted an early hypothesis and usually kept it, seldom correcting a wrong one.

title: JEPA for astronomy: multi-survey spectral alignment puts stellar parameters on the leading principal axes
abstract: Spectra from different surveys carry different systematics and are not calibrated against one another. Multi-survey foundation models for stellar spectra are then built by aligning embeddings of the same star observed across surveys. Most in astronomy follow the recipes established for language and vision, aligning with a contrastive loss that separates every star from the others. However, this does not ensure that the stellar physics is encoded in a form that a simple read-out can recover. Holding the cross-survey architecture fixed and varying only the alignment loss, we measure what an objective encodes from the principal-component geometry of the Gaia BP/RP (XP) spectra and from a linear probe of the stellar parameters. In a properly aligned embedding, the leading two principal components form a plane that recovers an analog of the Kiel diagram, the third component tracks [Fe/H], and [alpha/Fe] varies coherently across the plane, such that the chemically defined Galactic disks and accreted populations occupy distinct loci. We show that legibility, the ease of reading the information out, is highest for a training objective that never pushes stars apart, and instead constrains only the overall distribution of each survey's embeddings (JEPA). JEPA also exceeds the contrastive alternative at the same architecture, and the performance improves further as more surveys (Gaia XP+LAMOST LRS+DESI+APOGEE) are included. Predicted abundances for 8.0 million XP giants reproduce the main [alpha/Fe]-[Fe/H] structure of the Milky Way. These results indicate that the choice of alignment objective, not alignment alone, determines whether stellar labels are linearly recoverable.

title: Symmetry classification of hyperfine rovibrational molecular phase space
abstract: Symmetry-based structures have advanced molecular spectroscopy and quantum information science, yet connections between these fields remain largely unexplored. We construct a phase space theory of a molecule by jointly treating rotational, vibrational, and nuclear-spin degrees of freedom as the quotient of orientations and normal coordinates by the molecule's point group. The various combinations of how these three degrees of freedom transform under symmetries organize a molecule's states into molecular species, and we show that each species is defined by a particular absolutely maximally entangled (AME) carrier state, or, for 45 species, by a two-dimensional space of them. Up to local unitaries and the order of the sectors, molecular species realize 21 AME states across 75 point groups: a product state, four maximally entangled pairs, and 16 genuinely tripartite states. A Fourier transform on the quotient relates orientation and angular-momentum descriptions while preserving these carrier states. We propose an example experimental protocol for preparing and driving symmetry-adapted bend states of $\mathrm{CaOCH_3}$.

title: Analytical Interacting Tight-binding Model for Fractional Chern Insulators
abstract: We construct a two-dimensional 2-band tight-binding model with two-body interactions and without magnetic lattice translation, in which both the hopping and interaction are exponentially local (with Gaussian decay) in real space. The interaction is built from pair annihilation operators whose coefficients are hopping amplitudes divided by positive powers of relative distance. Without any band projection, the ground states at $1/3$ filling are exactly fractional Chern insulator (FCI) states (and thus have nonzero gap) for any finite lattice size with any periodic/twist boundary conditions. The FCI ground states are analogous to the discretized version of the Laughlin-like states in the continuum Chern-ideal band, though our FCI states do not require the onsite spinor structure that is necessary in the continuum. We further show analytically that, after adding one unit cell while keeping electron number fixed, the anyonic one-quasihole states are zero-energy ground states of the full Hamiltonian for any finite system size and any quasihole position, analogous to Laughlin quasiholes under the Haldane $V_1$ pseudopotential. Numerical evidence is provided for the possible nonzero gap of the FCI states at $1/3$ filling in the thermodynamic limit, when interaction strength is much smaller than the single-particle band gap.

title: Spin-free potential-energy curves, spectroscopic constants, and permanent dipole-moment functions for all 18 CO states correlating with the first atomic asymptote
